1) [Seif 1] One must be careful when performing hagalah, etc. The order of hagalah is as follows: take a large vessel filled with water and heat it until the water boils vigorously over the surface throughout the vessel, inside and outside. Insert the utensils one wishes to kasher, 1 at a time, one after another. Levush. Regarding a large utensil that cannot be inserted into the hagalah vessel, see below, seif 6.

2) Regarding how long the utensil should remain in the boiling water, Rif in Perek Kol Sha'ah writes that it should remain until it expels what it absorbed. Ran writes likewise, as do Rambam, chapter 5, law 23; Raavad in Sefer Tamim De'im, siman 25; and Rashba in Torat HaBayit, bayit 4, shaar 4. Radbaz, in Leshonot HaRambam, siman 241, also proves this from Rambam. Tur, however, writes that the custom is to insert them and remove them immediately, and writes likewise in Yoreh De'ah, siman 121. Mordechai, Perek Kol Sha'ah, siman 579, writes likewise, as cited by Beit Yosef; Levush, seif 2, likewise. Peri Chadash, at the end of seif 6, writes that the custom of Israel is Torah. Taz, seif katan 2, however, explains that Tur's word "immediately" is not literal: the utensil must remain at least a short time. Kol Bo likewise writes that one must not hurry to remove it before the boiling water has time to enter and expel what was absorbed. Eliyah Rabbah, letter 1; Shulchan Aruch HaRav, letter 4; Ben Ish Chai, Parashat Tzav, letter 12, write likewise. See below, letter 14.

3) One might ask: according to those who hold that one may not intentionally nullify a prohibition by Torah law, how did the Torah permit kashering the utensils of Midian by hagalah? Is he not intentionally nullifying the prohibited flavor absorbed in the utensils into the hagalah water? The answer is that the prohibition against intentional nullification applies where one intends to mix the prohibition into permitted food in order to benefit from it. Here his intent is to kasher the utensil and he derives no benefit from the prohibited substance itself, so it is permitted. Ran, Perek Ein Maamidin.

4) There, "before the fifth hour." At that time it is a secondary transfer of permitted flavor, even when the utensil is ben yomo. Taz, seif katan 1. The chametz imparts flavor to the utensil, the utensil to the water, and the water back to the bowl, while the prohibition of chametz has not yet taken effect. Mordechai, Perek Kol Sha'ah, siman 576; Levush, seif 3. Although some hold that because the designation "chametz" already rests upon it, it is considered prohibited absorption, and Maran took that view into account above in siman 451, seif 4, here he relies upon the lenient authorities because there are other authorities who independently permit these matters. Maamar Mordechai, letter 1. See above, siman 451, letter 39.

5) There, "before the fifth hour." This means before the beginning of the fifth hour, namely by the end of the fourth hour. Since chametz is at least rabbinically prohibited from the fifth hour, as stated above at the beginning of siman 443, it is no longer a secondary transfer of permitted flavor. Peri Chadash; Mateh Yehudah; Mekor Chaim, letter 1; Nehar Shalom, letter 1; Shulchan Aruch HaRav, letter 8; Chayei Adam, rule 125, letter 33.

6) There, "so that one will not need," etc. At that time one need not ensure that the utensil is not ben yomo. Even if it is ben yomo and the water does not contain 60 against the utensils, it is permitted, because chametz is still permitted and this is a secondary transfer of permitted flavor. Tosafos, Chullin 108b and Avodah Zarah 76a; Rosh at the end of Avodah Zarah and in Perek Kol Sha'ah; Mordechai, Perek Kol Sha'ah; Ran at the end of Perek Kol HaBasar. Tur and Beit Yosef cite them. Olat Shabbos, letter 1; Magen Avraham, seif katan 1; Chok Yaakov, letter 2; Chok Yosef, letter 1; Mekor Chaim, letter 2; Shulchan Aruch HaRav, letter 13; Chayei Adam there, letter 33, write likewise. Although Rama above in siman 447, seif 5, prohibits food cooked in a chametz utensil and does not rely upon secondary transfer of flavor, here there are several successive transfers, from the food to the utensil, from the utensil to the water, and from the water to the second utensil, and it is therefore permitted. Magen Avraham, Chok Yaakov, and Mekor Chaim there. This is the strict law. The custom, however, is not to kasher any utensil that is ben yomo, as stated below in Rama to seif 2. See also below, letter 21, regarding whether the hagalah vessel itself must first be kashered.

7) An incident occurred in which a piece of bread was found in the vessel in which utensils were being kashered before Pesach, and they asked whether the utensils had to undergo hagalah again. Beit David, siman 195, concludes that according to communities that do not apply chatichah na'asit neveilah, it is obvious that the utensils are not prohibited, because the flavor expelled by the bread into the water was nullified in 60. Even according to communities that apply chatichah na'asit neveilah, a second hagalah is unnecessary, because we have not seen that they accepted that stringency regarding mere flavor rather than tangible substance. Although they customarily kasher kneading utensils belonging to communities that are lenient, this is only initially. Since the entire matter is a custom, one should not add a new stringency. If, however, it is clearly established that their custom is to prohibit even after the fact because of flavor alone, then these utensils must certainly be kashered again. Zechor LeAvraham, end of siman 451. See above, siman 447, letters 59 and 76.

If the utensils are ben yomo. Even if a utensil is ben yomo and the water does not contain 60 against it, it is nevertheless permitted before the fifth hour because this is a secondary transfer of permitted flavor. After the fifth hour this rationale no longer applies. A difficulty arises from siman 447, seif 5, where Rama prohibits foods cooked in chametz utensils and does not permit them because of a secondary transfer of flavor. One may answer that here there are several transfers: from the food to the utensil, from the utensil to the water, and from the water to the second utensil; therefore it is permitted.

Whose absorption is slight. For example, spoons and cups. There is concern that they may absorb from what bowls and pots expel.

But many disagree, etc. The authorities differ whether one should insist upon 60 in the water, whether the utensils must be not ben yomo, and in what order the utensils should be inserted. The custom is to observe all the stringencies. The utensils should be cleaned thoroughly, allowed to remain unused for 24 hours, and kashered while the water is actively boiling.

One should first kasher utensils whose absorption is slight and afterward those whose absorption is greater. One should not keep a utensil in the water longer than necessary, and the water should not cease boiling. The hagalah vessel is kashered at the beginning and at the end. If the hagalah vessel itself is not ben yomo, it appears that technically it need not be kashered at the beginning, for it is no worse than the other utensils. If it was kashered at the beginning, it need not technically be kashered at the end when the utensils are not ben yomo. Nevertheless, the custom is to follow all the stringencies even before the fifth hour, as Bach writes.

A utensil should not be inserted when the water has stopped boiling. Those performing hagalah must therefore take care not to work so rapidly, one utensil immediately after another, that the boil is lost. Bowls and spoons, whose ordinary use is through pouring, have more room for leniency; a copper pot and other utensils used as a kli rishon require true kli rishon hagalah.

One should not pour water for hagalah by drawing it with another vessel from the boiling pot, because the drawn vessel is a kli sheini. If the drawing vessel is left inside the boiling pot until the water in it comes to a boil, it is considered a kli rishon. Mateh Moshe writes that hagalah should be done 3 days before Pesach; this depends upon custom. Sefer Chasidim, siman 730, writes that a Torah scholar expert in hagalah should conduct it.

One must be careful. Regarding the law after the fact, see Yoreh De'ah, siman 95, seif 3.

Together. Meaning that he inserts them at the same time into the hagalah vessel and there is not 60 in the water against any 1 of them.

Any ben yomo utensil. Even before the fifth hour, as a safeguard because of a utensil containing actual prohibited absorption, for which hagalah is ineffective while it is ben yomo if the water lacks 60, since the utensil can reabsorb from the hagalah water and the rationale of a secondary transfer of permitted flavor does not apply to actual prohibition. Even tables should be scrubbed thoroughly and left 24 hours after scrubbing so they are not ben yomo. They should be dry from cold water, lest the boiling water be cooled. One must pour upon them quickly and directly, not by casting the water through the air, which is not considered proper pouring. See Yoreh De'ah, siman 92. One should pour directly from the vessel in which the water was boiled and not draw it into a second vessel and then pour, because that is a kli sheini. If the drawing vessel remains inside the boiling vessel until the water in it itself boils, it has the status of a kli rishon. [Maharil] Mateh Moshe writes that hagalah should be performed 3 days before Pesach; all this depends upon custom. Sefer Chasidim, siman 730, states that a Torah scholar expert in hagalah should perform the hagalah.

2) Regarding how long a utensil should remain in the hagalah vessel, Rif in Perek Kol Sha'ah writes that it should remain until it expels what it absorbed. Ran writes likewise there, as do Rambam, chapter 5, law 23; Raavad in Sefer Tamim De'im, siman 25; and Rashba in Torat HaBayit, bayit 4, shaar 4. Radbaz, in Leshonot HaRambam, siman 241, likewise demonstrates that this is Rambam's view. Tur, however, writes that the custom is to insert them and remove them immediately, and writes likewise in Yoreh De'ah, siman 121. Mordechai, Perek Kol Sha'ah, siman 579, writes likewise, as cited by Beit Yosef. Levush, seif 2, also writes so. Peri Chadash, at the end of seif 6, writes that the custom of Israel is Torah. Taz, seif katan 2, explains that "immediately" is not literal; the utensil must remain at least briefly. Kol Bo likewise writes that one must not hurry to remove the utensil, so that the boiling water has time to enter and expel what was absorbed. Eliyah Rabbah, letter 1; Shulchan Aruch HaRav, letter 4; Ben Ish Chai, Parashat Tzav, letter 12, write likewise. See below, letter 14.
Taz, seif katan 11: The correct reading is: "if the utensil entered the hagalah vessel afterward, it is ineffective."

A rim around its mouth with clay. During the rest of the year one makes a dough rim, as stated in Perek Kol Sha'ah. Beit Hillel on Yoreh De'ah, siman 121, seif katan 1, writes in the name of Rosh that specifically regarding chametz before Pesach, where the utensil absorbed permitted matter, a rim is effective for a large utensil. For other prohibitions, however, a rim by itself is insufficient. The large utensil must first undergo hagalah once, and afterward, because of its lip, a rim is used. For chametz before Pesach, according to this view, the first hagalah is unnecessary before refilling it with boiling water and using the rim.

These words require study. Rif in the second chapter of Avodah Zarah, who cites the case of Mar Ukva, does not indicate this distinction, and neither does Rosh. The Rosh's statement about kashering the hagalah vessel twice concerns a vessel in which other utensils are kashered, which requires hagalah before and after, as the Mechaber writes above in seif 1. There is therefore no basis to distinguish this law between chametz and other prohibitions. The only clear difference is that during Pesach itself a dough rim cannot be relied upon, as appears from the Gemara and the halachic authorities.

The boiling water must rise over the utensil's rim. If a utensil is used also on its exterior, such as a bowl that is sometimes inverted over a pot, or a vessel used to draw food from a pot, its exterior likewise requires hagalah. Magen Avraham writes in the name of Maharil that a narrow-necked utensil that cannot be scrubbed inside, or a utensil containing tubes, cannot be kashered through hagalah.

6) There, "so that one will not need," etc. This means that before the fifth hour one need not ensure that the utensil is not ben yomo. Even if it is ben yomo and the water does not contain 60 against the utensils, it is permitted because chametz is still permitted and this is a secondary transfer of permitted flavor. Tosafos, Chullin 108b and Avodah Zarah 76a; Rosh at the end of Avodah Zarah and in Perek Kol Sha'ah; Mordechai, Perek Kol Sha'ah; Ran at the end of Perek Kol HaBasar. Tur and Beit Yosef cite them. Olat Shabbos, letter 1; Magen Avraham, seif katan 1; Chok Yaakov, letter 2; Chok Yosef, letter 1; Mekor Chaim, letter 2; Shulchan Aruch HaRav, letter 13; Chayei Adam, rule 125, letter 33, write likewise. Although Rama above in siman 447, seif 5, prohibits food cooked in a chametz utensil and does not rely on secondary transfer of flavor, here there are several transfers, from the food to the utensil, from the utensil to the water, and from the water to the second utensil, and it is therefore permitted. Magen Avraham, Chok Yaakov, and Mekor Chaim there. All this is the strict law, but the custom is not to kasher any utensil that is ben yomo, as stated below in Rama to seif 2. See below, letter 21, regarding whether the hagalah vessel itself must first be kashered.

7) An incident occurred in which a piece of bread was found in the hagalah vessel in which utensils were being kashered before Pesach, and they asked whether the utensils required hagalah a second time. Beit David, siman 195, concludes that according to communities that do not apply chatichah na'asit neveilah, it is obvious that the utensils are not prohibited, because the flavor expelled from the bread into the water was nullified in 60. Even according to communities that do apply chatichah na'asit neveilah, a second hagalah is unnecessary, because we have not seen that they accepted this rule regarding mere flavor as opposed to tangible substance. Although they customarily kasher kneading utensils belonging to communities that are lenient, this is only an initial stringency. Since the matter rests on custom, we should not add another stringency. If, however, it is clearly established that their custom is to prohibit even after the fact because of flavor alone, then these utensils certainly require hagalah again. See Beit David there; Zechor LeAvraham, end of siman 451; and above, siman 447, letters 59 and 76.
